prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed GLP-1 first, and I still think that is right on the merits and not just because of the agreement. It is an unusually complete chain from hormone physiology (Holst on human secretion and incretin action, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology, Mojsov on the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) form) through peptide pharmacology to long-acting agonists with documented glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit across many independent randomized trials. Maturity is not in doubt, and the clinical scale makes delay hard to defend. The three-name ceiling is met by the basic-science trio, which keeps the citation anchored in discovery.
statement.case_against: Credit is the weak point. Habener and other early peptide-identification contributors are not on the supplied list, Mojsov's priority is contested, and Knudsen's industrial development of liraglutide and semaglutide is what put the biology into patients. A trio of academic discoverers could be read as honouring physiology while leaving out the engineering that produced the drugs. This is a real tension rather than a formality, and the committee should not hide it behind the clean-sounding three.

responses.point: Perlmann proposes the three basic-science names for B012 and leaves the choice between honouring physiology and honouring industrial drug development unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with the trio but would not call the question closed. Native GLP-1 has a half-life of minutes, so the clinical transformation depends on the protraction chemistry Knudsen's group developed, and that is more than routine translation. My view is that a Nobel citation worded around the discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form is defensible, but only if we say openly that it does not capture the drug-engineering step. I would not accept a configuration that includes Knudsen at the price of Holst or Drucker; Holst's human physiology is the foundation.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks BCR-ABL inhibition (B016) second, as a paradigm of targeted therapy with two decades of survival data, and notes that it is overdue by timing alone.
responses.response: I accept that B016 is the most mature of the clinical candidates and that its patient impact is beyond dispute. I disagree on two points. The biological discovery of the target (Rowley, Witte, Konopka and others) is outside the credited names, so the prize would reward the drug programme while skipping the oncogene story. And B016 is essentially one drug in one disease, whereas GLP-1 has produced a class acting across diabetes, obesity and organ protection. I would keep B016 in view for a later year but do not put it above B009 or B024 for a second part.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks TNF blockade (B046) second, as a clean two-person bedside-to-bench story with decades of use, while asking whether the committee sees it as sufficiently basic.
responses.response: The Feldmann and Maini pairing is among the cleanest attributions on the list, and I do not doubt the clinical effect. My reservation is on the discovery step. The case that TNF is the dominant driver in rheumatoid synovium was built on a distinctive experimental argument, but the target biology and the antibody and fusion-protein engineering belong to many others, and the answer to your question about basic versus therapeutic contribution is unclear to me. I would put B046 behind B009 and B024, and I would be open to moving it if colleagues can show that the credited pair's contribution is more decisive than I currently see it.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B024 (unfolded protein response) second as the cleanest pairing, Walter and Mori, and treats optogenetics as hard to attribute.
responses.response: I agree that Walter and Mori is a clean pair and that B024 is the strongest basic-science alternative to B012. Where I would qualify is relevance to medicine: the clinical translation is still early, and a prize framed purely on cell-biological principle would sit better next to a clinically anchored part than on its own this year. On optogenetics, I share your concern that no three-person split is satisfactory, so I would not advance B022 as a primary proposal.

uncertainties: Whether a prize on GLP-1 should credit only the physiology and active-peptide discoverers or must also reflect the drug-development step by Knudsen.
How to weigh Mojsov's contested priority and the absence of Habener from the supplied names.
Whether a second part (B009 or B024) should share the prize or whether GLP-1 should stand alone.
For B009, how to handle the original chimeric receptor concept (Eshhar) outside the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate on the shortlist matches my research directly. I co-authored the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper, but that work is not a shortlisted discovery, and I have co-authored several papers with Rickard Sandberg, which is not a conflict with any shortlisted candidate. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted ballots.
